question: How is the flight control system operated?

options.text: Manually through mechanical linkage, using a control wheel for ailerons and elevator and pedals for the rudder
By hydraulic actuators controlled from the instrument panel
By fly-by-wire electric servos
By pneumatic actuators driven from engine bleed air

explanation: The flight control system consists of conventional aileron, rudder, and elevator surfaces, manually operated through mechanical linkage using a control wheel for ailerons/elevator and rudder/brake pedals for the rudder.

question: How is elevator trim accomplished, and which direction does forward rotation of the trim wheel produce?

options.text: Through an electric trim motor; forward rotation trims nose-up
Through a manually-operated elevator trim tab; forward rotation trims nose-down
Through a manually-operated elevator trim tab; forward rotation trims nose-up
Through aileron-linked trim only, with no dedicated elevator trim

explanation: A manually-operated elevator trim tab is provided; forward rotation of the trim wheel trims nose-down, and aft rotation trims nose-up.

question: What type of wing flaps are fitted, and how are they extended or retracted?

options.text: Fowler type, actuated by a manual crank
Split flaps, actuated pneumatically
Single-slot type, positioned by an electric switch lever on the instrument panel
Slotted flaps, deployed automatically by airspeed

explanation: The wing flaps are single-slot type and are extended or retracted by positioning the wing flap switch lever on the instrument panel to the desired deflection.

question: At what flap deflection positions does the wing flap switch lever have mechanical stops?
explanation: The flap switch lever moves in a slot with mechanical stops at the 10° and 20° positions; for settings greater than 10°, the lever is moved to the right to clear the stop.

question: What amperage circuit breaker protects the wing flap system, and how is it labeled?

options.text: 15-ampere, labeled FLAP
5-ampere, labeled WING
30-ampere, labeled TRIM
10-ampere, labeled AILERON

explanation: The wing flap system circuit is protected by a 15-ampere circuit breaker, labeled FLAP, on the right side of the instrument panel.

question: How is flap travel in degrees indicated to the pilot?

options.text: By a digital readout on the annunciator panel
By a scale and pointer on the left side of the flap switch lever
There is no flap position indication; position is judged visually out the window
By a needle on the airspeed indicator

explanation: A scale and pointer on the left side of the flap switch lever indicates flap travel in degrees.

question: What flap setting is used for a normal takeoff?

options.text: Flaps must be fully retracted
30° fixed

explanation: Normal takeoffs are accomplished with wing flaps at 0° - 10°, per the Normal Takeoff checklist.

question: For a short field landing, what flap setting is used, and below what airspeed should flaps be extended?

options.text: 10°, extended below 100 KIAS
20°, extended below 111 KIAS
0°, flaps not used for short field landings
30°, extended below 85 KIAS

explanation: The Short Field Landing checklist calls for wing flaps 30°, extended below 85 KIAS, the maximum flap extended speed.

question: What is a control lock designed to prevent, and what warning flag does it display?

options.text: Wind buffeting damage while parked; a red flag labeled CONTROL LOCK, REMOVE BEFORE STARTING ENGINE
In-flight control jamming; a green flag labeled SAFE TO FLY
Accidental flap retraction; a yellow flag labeled FLAPS LOCKED
Brake failure while parked; a red flag labeled BRAKES SET

explanation: The control lock locks the ailerons and elevator in neutral to prevent wind-buffeting damage while parked, and carries a red flag labeled CONTROL LOCK, REMOVE BEFORE STARTING ENGINE, placed over the ignition switch when installed.

question: What construction feature distinguishes the ailerons from the flaps, though both use a similar sheet-metal rib and skin structure?

options.text: The flaps contain balance weights; the ailerons do not
The ailerons contain balance weights in their forward spar; the flaps do not, but add a formed leading edge section
The ailerons are fabric-covered; the flaps are all-metal
There is no construction difference between ailerons and flaps

explanation: The ailerons are constructed with a forward spar containing balance weights; the flaps are built basically the same way but without balance weights, adding instead a formed sheet metal leading edge section.

question: Where is the ground-adjustable trim tab located on the empennage?

options.text: On the leading edge of the horizontal stabilizer
On the tip of the vertical stabilizer
At the base of the rudder's trailing edge
On the elevator's leading edge

explanation: The rudder is constructed with a ground adjustable trim tab at the base of its trailing edge.

question: Which half of the elevator forms the elevator trim tab?

options.text: The entire trailing edge of the left half forms the trim tab
Both halves share a single center-mounted trim tab
There is no elevator trim tab; trim is achieved by spring bias only
The entire trailing edge of the right half of the elevator is hinged and forms the trim tab

explanation: The elevator's left half has a formed trailing edge skin, while the entire trailing edge of the right half is hinged and forms the elevator trim tab.

question: During a balked landing (go-around), to what flap setting are the flaps reduced immediately after full power is applied, before final retraction?

options.text: 0°, straight to fully retracted

explanation: In a balked landing climb, wing flaps are retracted to 20° immediately after full power is applied, then slowly retracted fully once a safe airspeed is reached.

question: Rudder pedal extensions, when installed, consist of what parts?

options.text: A hydraulic cylinder and two mounting bolts
A rudder pedal face, two spacers, and two spring clips
A telescoping rod and a locking pin
An adjustable bracket bolted through the firewall

explanation: Rudder/brake pedal extensions consist of a rudder pedal face, two spacers, and two spring clips that snap over the top and bottom of the existing pedal.
